plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single vector-field plot inside a square frame. The horizontal axis is labeled "x (m)" with ticks from -2 to 4, the vertical axis "y (m)" with ticks from -2 to 2. The field appears as a regular grid of dark blue arrows whose lengths vary sharply with position, shrinking toward the edges of the frame until they read as bare dots. Two centers of activity stand out, both on the line y = 0. Around the origin the arrows are long and point radially outward in every direction. Around the point at x = 2, y = 0 they are just as long but point radially inward, converging on that spot. Between and around the pair they take intermediate directions, turning from the outward pattern on the left into the inward pattern on the right and shortening with distance from either center. No source objects or charge symbols are drawn; the arrows alone stand for the field. Packing direction and magnitude into hundreds of separate arrows is what makes the pattern dense and awkward to follow. The plot motivates replacing the grid with continuous field lines that carry the same information without the clutter.

interactionPlan.concept: A dipole electric field can be shown either as many local vector samples or as continuous field lines, and each local arrow is the vector sum of the fields from the positive and negative charges.
elements: square plotting frame
horizontal x-axis labeled 'x (m)' with ticks from -2 to 4
vertical y-axis labeled 'y (m)' with ticks from -2 to 2
regular grid of dark blue electric-field arrows
very short dot-like arrows near the outer edges of the plot
outward radial arrow pattern centered at x = 0, y = 0 representing the positive charge region
inward radial arrow pattern centered at x = 2, y = 0 representing the negative charge region
intermediate curved direction pattern between the two charge centers
optional positive charge marker '+q' at x = 0, y = 0 for explanatory overlay
optional negative charge marker '-q' at x = 2, y = 0 for explanatory overlay
continuous dark blue electric field lines starting near the positive charge and ending near the negative charge
arrowheads on field lines showing direction from positive toward negative
hover-highlighted enlarged local field arrow
hover readout box showing local field magnitude |E|
hover contribution arrow from the positive charge labeled 'E from +q'
hover contribution arrow from the negative charge labeled 'E from -q'
hover resultant arrow labeled 'net E'

interactions.label: Representation
interactions.teaches: The vector grid and field-line drawing encode the same dipole direction pattern, but field lines reveal the overall flow from positive to negative charge with less visual clutter
Any displayed arrow is the local net electric field: the vector sum of the contribution from the positive charge and the contribution from the negative charge

interactions.label: Sampling density
interactions.teaches: Changing the number of sample arrows changes only how crowded the representation looks; the underlying dipole field pattern remains the same

demo_steps.title: Read the vector grid
demo_steps.narration: The arrows point away from the source near the origin and into the source near x = 2, showing a positive-negative charge pair. Arrow length shows field strength, so the arrows shrink into dots far from the charges.

demo_steps.title: Inspect one local arrow
demo_steps.narration: Hover over a grid point to enlarge that arrow. The contribution arrows show that the visible field arrow is not from one charge alone, but the vector sum of the fields from both charges.

demo_steps.title: Separate field from sampling
demo_steps.narration: Move the sampling-density slider: sparse and dense grids show the same dipole pattern. The clutter changes because the sampling changes, not because the electric field changes.

demo_steps.title: Switch to field lines
demo_steps.narration: Field lines replace hundreds of arrows with continuous paths that follow the same local directions. The lines run from the positive region to the negative region, making the dipole structure easier to follow.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The dense arrow grid is just a sampled representation of one continuous dipole field: every local arrow is a vector sum, and field lines trace the same directions more cleanly.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use an SVG-style 2D plot with a square black frame and white background. Keep the x-axis labeled x (m) with ticks -2 through 4 and the y-axis labeled y (m) with ticks -2 through 2. Draw dark navy arrows on a regular grid; arrows are longest near (0,0) and (2,0), radiate outward from (0,0), converge inward toward (2,0), and become tiny dots near the plot edges. In field-line mode, fade the grid arrows and show smooth dark blue curves with arrowheads running from the positive charge region at the origin toward the negative charge region at x = 2. Charge markers should be subtle explanatory overlays rather than dominant objects, since the original figure shows the field arrows alone.

authoredContext:
This diagram is correct, but it becomes less useful as the source charge distribution becomes more complicated. For example, consider the vector field diagram of a dipole (the figure).

The vector field of a dipole. Even with just two identical charges, the vector field diagram becomes difficult to understand.

A vector plot of the electric field due to two sources. The sources are not shown. The field is represented by arrows in an x y graph. Both x and y are in meters and both scales are from -2 meters to 4 meters. Near the origin, the arrows are long and point away from it. Near the point at coordinates 2, 0 the arrows are long and point toward the point. The arrows get smaller as we move farther from those two location and point in intermediate directions.

There is a more useful way to present the same information. Rather than drawing a large number of increasingly smaller vector arrows, we instead connect all of them together, forming continuous lines and curves, as shown in the figure.

evaluation.notes: The generated figure correctly captures the dipole vector field, axes, ticks, colors, and labels, but the default sampling density and arrow scaling make it look more cluttered and less like the source.
action_items: Reduce the default sampling density to better match the source grid spacing.
Increase the minimum visible size/opacity of far-field arrows so they resemble the source's small blue marks rather than nearly disappearing dots.
Tone down the longest near-charge arrows so the local starburst effect is less exaggerated.
If the goal is a static drop-in replacement, make the control panel collapsible or less visually dominant by default.
